steps.tx: The **Thomas splint** was introduced by Hugh Owen Thomas in 1875 for managing tuberculosis of the knee and hip, and later revolutionized the survival of open femoral shaft fractures in wartime. The device consists of an oval padded leather ring connected to two unequal parallel side bars joined distally by a notched W-crossbar, maintaining traction while stabilizing the thigh.
steps.say: Hugh Owen Thomas designed this splint in 1875 to treat joint tuberculosis. In World War One, using it for femoral fractures reduced mortality from eighty percent to under twenty percent. An oval padded ring fits against the ischial tuberosity while two side bars carry traction to the foot.

vis.title: Thomas Splint Components
rows: Slopes at 120 degrees, abuts ischial tuberosity
Outer bar bows outward over trochanter
Framework for slings and knee flexion

steps.tx: Walk around this splint as you would at the bedside. The padded ring sits snugly against the ischial tuberosity, two side bars run down the leg, and a Pearson attachment supports the knee while cords carry traction from the foot end. Seeing the assembled **Thomas splint** explains how it both immobilises a femoral fracture and applies steady pull.
steps.say: This Thomas splint shows its padded ring at the ischial tuberosity, side bars, knee support and traction cords together. Assembled this way it immobilises a femoral fracture while applying steady traction.

vis.alt: Thomas splint assembly showing a padded oval ring against the ischial tuberosity, side bars, Pearson attachment and distal traction cord

steps.tx: Accurate **splint measurement** prevents pressure necrosis over the perineum and ensures adequate distal limb extension. Ring circumference must equal the uppermost thigh circumference plus five centimeters, allowing the ring to pass freely yet rest firmly against the ischial tuberosity. The length is measured from the groin to the heel plus fifteen to twenty centimeters, leaving working space for the distal crossbar.
steps.say: Measure the ring circumference at the highest thigh fold and add five centimeters so it clears the groin without pinching. For length, measure from the perineum down to the heel and add fifteen to twenty centimeters. This extra distal length ensures room for the pulley cord and weight attachments.

left.title: Ring Sizing Formula
points: Add 5 cm or 2 inches for soft tissue ease
Ensures ring rests against ischial tuberosity

right.title: Length Sizing Formula
points: Measure from perineal groin to heel
Add 15 to 20 cm or 6 to 8 inches
Provides working room for traction cords

steps.tx: In **fixed traction**, skin extension tapes or skeletal cords tie directly to the notched distal end of the splint, and a Spanish windlass twists the ties taut. Countertraction is generated directly as the proximal ring impacts against the patient's rigid ischial tuberosity. This self-contained setup is ideal during emergency transfer and military evacuations because it requires no overhead pulleys or dangling weights.
steps.say: In fixed traction, traction tapes tie directly to the notched crossbar of the splint, tightened with a wooden stick known as a Spanish windlass. The ring pushes firmly against the ischial tuberosity for countertraction. This self-contained traction is ideal during ambulance transport.

vis.title: Traction Modalities Comparison
rows: Body weight against tilted bed foot
Weights hung via overhead Balkan frame
Definitive ward care with Pearson attachment

steps.tx: In **sliding traction**, the splint is suspended from an overhead Balkan beam, and the ring floats freely off the perineum without abutment. Skeletal traction cords run over pulleys to suspended weights, roughly ten percent of body weight for a femoral shaft break. Tilting the foot of the bed upwards twenty centimeters enlists patient body weight to generate smooth, continuous countertraction.
steps.say: For sliding or balanced traction, hang the splint from an overhead frame with a Pearson attachment that permits knee motion. The ring stays completely free of the skin. Countertraction comes from tilting the bed foot twenty centimeters, using the patient's own body weight against the traction weights.

left.title: Suspension Mechanics
points: Splint suspended via Balkan overhead frame
Padded ring floats free of groin skin

right.title: Weight and Tilt Values
points: Traction weight is 10 percent body weight
Patient body weight acts as countertraction

steps.tx: The standard **pin insertion** site for adult femoral fractures is the proximal tibia, located two centimeters posterior and two centimeters distal to the tibial tubercle. Inserting a Denham or Steinmann pin strictly from lateral to medial protects the common peroneal nerve winding around the fibular neck. Daily pin-site chlorhexidine cleansing prevents secondary pin-track osteomyelitis.
steps.say: Insert the skeletal traction pin through the proximal tibia, two centimeters below and two centimeters behind the tibial tubercle. Always push the pin from lateral to medial to protect the common peroneal nerve. Clean the pin skin interface daily with chlorhexidine to stop track infection.

quiz.q: What provides countertraction when using fixed traction in a Thomas splint?
options: Pressure of the padded ring against the ischial tuberosity
Overhead weights suspended from a Balkan frame
Elevation of the foot of the bed by twenty centimeters
A pelvic binder anchored to the mattress
quiz.explain: In fixed traction, traction cords are tied to the distal notch of the splint and counterforce is provided by the upper ring pushing directly against the rigid ischial tuberosity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended direction for inserting a proximal tibial traction pin?
options: Lateral to medial, 2 cm distal and posterior to tibial tubercle
Medial to lateral, directly through the tibial tubercle
Anterior to posterior, through the patellar tendon
Medial to lateral, 5 cm distal to the joint line
quiz.explain: Inserting the pin from lateral to medial protects the vulnerable common peroneal nerve as it curves around the neck of the fibula on the lateral aspect.
